sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The systemd journal is systemd's own logging system. It is equivalent to syslog in the init system. It collects and stores kernel logging data, system log messages, standard output, and errors for various systemd services. The thing with logging is that over time, it starts to grow big. If you check the disk space in Linux, you'll see that sometimes it takes several GB of space.

sections.heading: By unit
sections.text: To follow journal entries for a specific unit in real time: sudo journalctl -f -u cups where -f shows only recent journal entries and -u allows specifying the unit name (e.g. cups ).

sections.heading: By time
sections.text: To query entries within a specific time window: sudo journalctl --since "2024-10-11 00:30:00" --until "2024-10-11 03:00:00" where --since and --until act as lower and upper time boundaries respectively.

sections.heading: Check disk space
sections.text: First, check the space taken by journal logs with the du command: du -sh /var/log/journal/ You can also use journalctl directly for the same purpose: journalctl --disk-usage

sections.heading: Rotate
sections.text: The first recommended step is to rotate journal files. This marks currently active journal logs as archives and creates fresh log files. It is optional but considered good practice. sudo journalctl --rotate

sections.heading: Clear journal logs older than N days
sections.text: Keep in mind that logs are important for auditing purposes, so avoid deleting all of them at once. To remove all entries older than two days: sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2d

sections.heading: Restrict logs to a certain size
sections.text: Another approach is to restrict the total log size. This deletes journal log files until the disk space occupied falls below the specified threshold. sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=100M

sections.heading: Restrict number of log files
sections.text: The third method limits the number of archived log files. As logs grow older they are archived into separate files. To keep only five archive files: journalctl --vacuum-files=5

sections.heading: Automatically clearing old log files
sections.text: The manual vacuum operations above clean the logs at the time of execution. In a month, logs will accumulate again. Rather than relying on manual intervention, systemd can be configured to handle old log files automatically. The configuration file is located at /etc/systemd/journald.conf . Lines that are commented out indicate the compiled-in defaults (they are in effect even when commented). The most relevant settings for automatic housekeeping are: Setting Description SystemMaxUse Maximum disk space that journal logs may occupy SystemMaxFileSize Maximum size of an individual journal log file SystemMaxFiles Maximum number of journal log files to keep Make a backup of the configuration file before editing: cp /etc/systemd/journald.conf /etc/systemd/journald.conf.back Uncomment (remove the leading # ) the setting you want to activate. The example below restricts the maximum journal disk space to 250 MB: # This file is part of systemd. # # systemd is free software; you can redistribute it and/or modify it # under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by # the Free Software Foundation; either version 2.1 of the License, or # (at your option) any later version. # # Entries in this file show the compile time defaults. # You can change settings by editing this file. # Defaults can be restored by simply deleting this file. # # See journald.conf(5) for details. [Journal] #Storage=auto #Compress=yes #Seal=yes #SplitMode=uid #SyncIntervalSec=5m #RateLimitIntervalSec=30s #RateLimitBurst=1000 SystemMaxUse=250M #SystemKeepFree= #SystemMaxFileSize= #SystemMaxFiles=100 After editing the configuration, restart the journal daemon to apply the changes: sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald NOTE: journald.conf allows further tuning beyond housekeeping, including setting the minimum log level (e.g. info , debug , err ). Refer to man journald.conf for the full parameter reference.
